title: Git and GitHub workflow
summary: Commits as save points, branches as safe sandboxes, pull requests as the door to production, and how to undo a bad change without panic.
youWillLearn: Why a commit is a save point you can always return to
How to undo a bad change with git revert
How branches keep unfinished work away from the live app
What a pull request adds: a preview, checks and a second pair of eyes
Why a leaked secret needs more than a revert

glossary.GitHub: A website that stores a copy of your project's code and its history, and where changes are reviewed.
glossary.production: The live version of the app, the one real users open.
glossary.Git: A program on your laptop that records every saved version of the project's files.
glossary.repository: The project folder plus its full history of changes. Your laptop has a copy, GitHub has a copy.
glossary.commit: A saved snapshot of your files with a short message and a unique id, like a named save point in a game.
glossary.branch: A separate line of commits where you can work without touching the main line.
glossary.main: The branch that holds the real, approved version of the app. On Vercel, pushing to it deploys production.
glossary.push: Upload your new commits from your laptop to GitHub.
glossary.pull request: A page on GitHub that asks to merge one branch into another, with the diff, comments, checks and a preview link.
glossary.diff: The exact lines added and removed by a change, shown in red and green.
glossary.merge: Bring the commits of one branch into another, so both lines of work become one.
glossary.revert: A new commit that does the exact opposite of an old one. It undoes the change without erasing history.
glossary.force push: Overwriting the history on GitHub with your local version. It can silently delete other people's commits.

steps.title: How a change reaches Notely today
body: You build Notely, our notes app, with Claude Code on your laptop. When a change looks done, Claude Code uploads the files straight to Vercel, the company that runs Notely.
Vercel puts them on the app server (the computer running Notely's code), replacing what was there. That live version is called production. Nothing else keeps track of the changes.

scene.caption: Files go straight from the laptop to the live app server. No save points yet.

steps.title: It worked yesterday
body: You ask Claude Code to add tags to notes. It edits fourteen files, and they go straight to production. Now the Summarize button throws an error.
Which of the fourteen changes broke it? What did the files look like yesterday? Nothing recorded the changes one by one, so you can only guess and patch on top of the damage.

callout.text: Editing a Figma file with version history turned off. One bad hour of changes, and there is no "restore this version" button.

changes: ~ Laptop: fourteen files changed in one go
~ App Server: Summarize is broken
~ Live app Working → Broken

scene.caption: Fourteen changed files go live at once, and something in them breaks the app.

steps.title: Commits: save points with names
body: Git, a program on your laptop, fixes this with commits. A commit is a snapshot of the whole project, with a message and an id like 7c2e.
Replay the same work with Git: each change becomes a commit in the project's history, its repository. Yesterday is one step back.

callout.text: Claude Code creates commits for you when you ask it to. You still decide when a save point is worth making: after each small, working change.

changes: − Laptop and App Server: we zoom into the history
+ Notes list, AI summary, Add tags: three commits in a row
~ Save points 0 → 3

scene.caption: The same work, saved as three commits. The newest one is broken; the one before it still exists.

steps.title: Undo with revert, not by hand
body: Production is broken. Do not start editing files in a hurry. Use revert.

git revert creates a new commit that does the exact opposite of the bad one. The history stays complete. Push it to GitHub (a website that stores the code, which Vercel now deploys from), and the app is back to how it was before tags.

code.code:
git log --oneline -5   # find the bad commit
git revert e91b        # new commit that undoes it
git push               # send it up, Vercel deploys it
code.caption: Claude Code can run these too. Ask it to revert, not to "fix it quickly".

changes: + Revert tags: a new commit that undoes Add tags
+ App Server: runs the newest commit, working again
~ Save points 3 → 4
~ Live app Broken → Working

scene.caption: The revert is one more commit. The broken change is undone, and still in history.

steps.title: Branches: work beside the live app
body: Now you redo tags, safely. A branch is a separate line of commits. Main holds what is live. New work goes on its own branch, here feature/tags.
You can commit half-finished tags all afternoon. Production keeps running main, untouched, until you decide the work is ready.

callout.text: Duplicating a page in Figma to explore a new layout. The original stays clean for the client, and you bring the good ideas back later.

changes: − Notes list, AI summary, Add tags: older history steps back
+ Tag chips, Tag filter: commits on a new branch
+ Two lanes: main and feature/tags
~ Save points 4 → 6

scene.caption: Tags grow on their own branch. The app server still runs main.

steps.title: Small commits, clear messages
body: A good commit does one thing: "Show tag chips", then "Filter by tag". When something breaks, small commits point straight at the cause.
Before each commit, read the diff: every line added and removed. Then push the branch to GitHub, so the work is backed up off the laptop.

callout.text: When two branches change the same lines, Git stops and asks which version wins: a merge conflict. Short-lived branches keep them rare. If Claude Code resolves one, read the result; it can quietly drop the other side's change.

code.code:
git switch -c feature/tags      # new branch
git diff                        # read every line
git add src/components/TagChip.tsx
git commit -m "Show tag chips on notes"
git push -u origin feature/tags
code.caption: -u links the local branch to the one on GitHub, so later a plain git push is enough.

changes: ~ Tag chips, Tag filter: pushed to GitHub as a backup

scene.caption: Each small commit on the branch is pushed to GitHub as a backup.

steps.title: Pull requests: the door to main
body: When the branch is ready, you open a pull request on GitHub: a page asking to bring the branch into main, with the full diff.
Then, on their own, Checks run: small programs that test the code. Vercel builds a preview: a copy of this branch at its own web address. Nothing goes live until someone presses Merge.

callout.text: Working alone? Still use pull requests. The preview link is free QA, and the pull request page is a written record a client can read.

changes: − Revert tags, Tag chips, Tag filter, lanes: the branch is one block
+ Tags Branch → Pull Request: asks to join main
+ Checks and Preview: run on their own for the request
~ App Server waits: nothing is merged yet

scene.caption: The pull request gathers checks and a preview before anything goes live.

steps.title: Letting Claude Code drive Git
body: Claude Code can run the whole loop: branch, small commits, push, and open the pull request with gh, GitHub's command line tool.
Your job moves from typing commands to reviewing. You read the diff like a design crit, click through the preview, wait for green checks, and only then let it merge.

code.code:
gh pr create --title "Add tags to notes" \
  --body "Adds tags column, chips and filter"
gh pr checks --watch  # wait for green
gh pr merge --squash  # one tidy commit on main
code.caption: --squash folds the branch's commits into one commit on main, which is simple to revert later.

callout.text: Ask it to work on a branch, never on main. Check the diff for files you did not expect: lockfiles, config, database changes, .env. Are commit messages specific? Did it push with --force? If so, ask why.

changes: + You: read the diff and click through the preview
~ Checks green, Pull Request merged into main
~ App Server deploys the new main

scene.caption: Checks are green and the preview looks right, so the pull request merges and main goes live.

steps.title: Secrets in history stay in history
body: Say the Add tags commit also held .env.local, the file with Notely's Claude API key (its password for the AI). Reverting removes the file from the newest version only; the old commit still holds the key, forever.
Treat it as leaked and rotate it: make a new key, delete the old. List the file in .gitignore so Git skips it.

callout.text: Do not rewrite shared history with a force push to hide it. Copies already exist on GitHub and other laptops, and bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes. Rotating the key is the real fix.

changes: − You, Tags Branch, Pull Request, Checks, Preview, App Server
+ Add tags, Revert tags: two commits on main
+ .env.local: a secret file still inside Add tags

scene.caption: The revert removed the file from main, but the old commit still holds the key.

steps.title: Recap: save, undo, branch, review
body: Commits are named save points, and git revert undoes a bad one with a new commit. Branches keep new work away from main, which is what production runs. A pull request adds checks, a preview and a review before merging.
A leaked secret is the exception: no commit can take it back. Rotate it.
changes: ~ .env.local: key rotated, the old copy is now useless

scene.caption: History keeps everything, so a leaked key is replaced, not hidden.

quiz.question: A merged pull request broke production ten minutes ago. A teammate already has the new main on their laptop. What is the safest way to undo it?

options.text: git reset --hard to the old commit, then force push main.
options.why: That rewrites shared history. Your teammate's copy no longer matches GitHub, and their next push can bring the bad commit back or lose work.

options.text: Edit the broken files by hand until the error goes away.
options.why: Patching under pressure often adds new bugs, and the app stays broken while you work.

options.text: Revert the pull request, which adds a new commit that undoes it.
options.why: A revert is a normal commit on top of main. Production returns to the old behavior, history stays intact, and you can fix the bug calmly on a branch.

quiz.question: Claude Code opened a pull request called "Add tags". The diff also changes supabase/migrations, package-lock.json and middleware.ts. What do you do?

options.text: Ask why each unexpected file changed before merging.
options.why: A migration changes the live database and middleware runs on every request. Each one needs a reason that fits the feature. The lockfile change may be fine if a package was added on purpose.

options.text: Merge it. The checks are green, so it must be fine.
options.why: Checks only catch what they test. They cannot tell whether a change belongs in this pull request at all.

options.text: Close the pull request and write the feature yourself.
options.why: Unexpected files are a question, not proof of a bad change. Asking is faster and you learn what changed.

quiz.question: You notice you committed .env.local with a live API key and pushed it. You revert the commit. Are you safe?

options.text: Yes. The revert removed the file.
options.why: It removed the file from the newest version only. The old commit still contains the key, and anyone with the repository can read it.

options.text: No. Create a new key, delete the old one, and ignore the file.
options.why: Once a secret is pushed, assume it is leaked. Rotating the key makes the leaked copy worthless, and .gitignore stops it happening again.

options.text: Yes, as long as the repository is private.
options.why: Private repositories still get cloned, shared with tools and opened to collaborators. Private lowers the risk; it does not undo the leak.

takeaways: A commit is a named snapshot. Small commits with clear messages make bugs quick to find.
Undo a bad change with git revert, never with a force push on shared branches.
Do new work on a branch. main is what production runs.
A pull request gives you automatic checks, a preview and a diff to review before merging.
A secret that was ever committed is leaked. Rotate it, then add the file to .gitignore.
